answerText: Yes. SBS (styrene-butadiene-styrene) modified-bitumen membrane can blister over a concrete roof primarily because air and/or moisture becomes trapped beneath or between membrane layers, and heat causes the trapped vapor/air to expand. The problem is often compounded by inadequate adhesion or voids created during installation. Main causes Moisture in the concrete substrate Concrete contains moisture for a long time after placement, and moisture can also enter through cracks, leaks, or wet insulation/underlayment. When the membrane is relatively vapor-impermeable, moisture cannot readily escape. Solar heating raises the temperature of the concrete and trapped moisture, increasing vapor pressure and pushing the membrane upward. Research specifically examining concrete substrates found that concrete moisture condition and air permeability are major factors controlling blistering pressure . J J-STAGE Trapped air or water vapor in installation voids A small void between the SBS membrane and concrete—or between membrane plies—can become a blister. The National Research Council of Canada found that gases inside actual SBS roof blisters consisted primarily of air and water vapor . It concluded that temperature changes can produce a cyclic "pumping" effect that enlarges the blister. N NRC Publications Poor or incomplete adhesion If the membrane isn't continuously bonded to the substrate, isolated pockets are created. With hot-applied SBS systems, causes can include insufficient asphalt coverage, improper asphalt viscosity/application temperature, poor wetting, or uncoated areas. NRC/NRCA investigations identified failure surfaces associated with discontinuities in the mopping asphalt and uncoated spots , with improper viscosity and inadequate wetting contributing to the problem. N National Roofing Contractors Association Wet conditions during installation Installing over a damp concrete deck or wet materials can effectively seal that moisture beneath a vapor-resistant membrane. NRC guidance specifically identifies entrapped moisture, uneven substrates, and gaps in bitumen application as causes of blisters. N NRC Publications Uneven concrete or surface irregularities Depressions, ridges, rough concrete, curing compounds, dust, laitance, or other contaminants can prevent full contact. Those areas can become localized voids that later inflate. Solar heating and daily temperature cycling A dark SBS membrane can become very hot in direct sun. The resulting temperature increase raises the pressure of trapped air and water vapor. Cooling then reduces the pressure, producing repeated expansion/contraction cycles that can progressively enlarge a blister. N NRC Publications +1 Why concrete roofs are particularly susceptible A concrete deck can act as a reservoir for moisture . If an impermeable SBS membrane is installed before the concrete has adequately dried—or if moisture subsequently enters the assembly—the membrane can effectively trap that moisture. A simplified sequence is: Moist concrete → SBS membrane installed → moisture/air trapped → sun heats roof → vapor pressure increases → adhesion locally fails → membrane lifts → blister grows. Importantly, a blister doesn't necessarily mean that the SBS membrane itself is defective . NRC testing found that blister formation did not appear to depend on the tensile strength of the SBS membrane; the conditions beneath/within the membrane system were more important. N NRC Publications Particularly useful sources National Research Council Canada — “Blistering in SBS Polymer Modified Bituminous Roofs” : A concise technical discussion of causes, prevention, and treatment. N NRC Publications NRC publication nrc-publications.canada.ca NRC/NRCA — “Investigating the Cause of Blistering in SBS Polymer Modified-Bitumen Roofing Membranes” : The most useful source for understanding what is actually inside SBS blisters and how they develop. N NRC Publications Full technical report nrc-publications.canada.ca NRCA — “Investigating the Cause of Blistering…” : The NRCA-hosted version discusses installation issues such as mopping skips, viscosity, wetting, and uncoated areas. N National Roofing Contractors Association NRCA technical report nrca.net NRCA — “The Lightning Round” (2024) : Discusses the history of blistering problems with mop-applied SBS cap sheets and subsequent changes in application practices. N National Roofing Contractors Association NRCA article nrca.net Concrete substrate research : Experimental research specifically investigating membrane blistering over concrete found that moisture and air permeability of the concrete affect the pressure responsible for blistering . J J-STAGE Research paper on concrete and membrane blistering jstage.jst.go.jp If you're investigating an actual blister The most useful diagnostic information is where the blister is located in the roof assembly . For example, whether it is: between concrete and the base sheet, between two SBS plies, between base sheet and cap sheet, concentrated over a concrete crack/joint, concentrated in areas of ponding water, or appearing uniformly over a large portion of the roof. If you tell me how the SBS roof was installed (torch-applied, hot-mopped, cold-adhered, or self-adhered), the approximate age of the concrete, and where the blisters are occurring , I can narrow this down to the most likely cause and explain how to distinguish trapped moisture from installation-related voids . answerText: Blisters in a torch-applied bitumen membrane are usually caused by trapped air or moisture between layers , inadequate adhesion, or vapor pressure from the roof assembly. The correct repair depends on whether the blister is superficial and intact or has split/opened. For a small, intact blister A roofing professional will generally: Inspect the blister and surrounding membrane. Check whether it is actually loose from the substrate and whether moisture is present underneath. Don't simply torch the bubble flat—this can damage the membrane and may trap moisture elsewhere. Cut the blister open if the membrane is delaminated. A controlled slit or cross-cut is made through the affected membrane, allowing the trapped air/moisture to escape. The extent of the cut should be determined by how far the membrane has lost adhesion. Allow wet materials to dry. If water has entered the roof assembly, the wet material needs to be removed/replaced or adequately dried before closing the repair. Otherwise, the blister is likely to return. Re-adhere the membrane using the manufacturer's approved method. For a torch-applied APP/SBS membrane, this generally means carefully heat-welding compatible modified-bitumen material. GAF's installation guidance, for example, specifies uniform heating and warns against overheating because it can damage the membrane. It also requires continuous adhesion at seams. G GAF Patch over the repaired area with compatible membrane. The patch should extend substantially beyond the damaged/cut area and be fully bonded around its perimeter. Use the same membrane system, or one specifically approved by the membrane manufacturer. GAF notes that modified-bitumen membrane can be used to patch small cracks and holes in existing torch-down roofing. G GAF Seal and finish the repair properly. Any exposed reinforcement, seams, edges, or details should be treated according to the membrane manufacturer's repair specification. A compatible modified-bitumen flashing cement may be appropriate for certain details, but it shouldn't be used as a substitute for repairing a large delamination. G GAF If there are many blisters If you're seeing numerous blisters, large blisters, recurring blisters, or blisters containing water , don't just patch each one. That can indicate a problem with the underlying roof assembly—such as moisture in the insulation/deck, inadequate vapor control, poor adhesion, or inadequate ventilation. In that situation, a roofer should make test cuts/core samples to determine how deep the problem goes. If the underlying layers are wet or extensively delaminated, portions of the roof may need to be removed and replaced rather than simply re-torched. Important safety point Torch-applied roofing involves an open propane flame and can ignite combustible roof components or concealed materials. GAF specifically calls for fire-watch procedures, review of combustible substrates, appropriate propane-equipment handling, and trained installers. G GAF +1 I therefore wouldn't recommend trying to heat a blister flat yourself, particularly on a wood-decked roof or where the construction below the membrane isn't known. In the U.S., GAF also notes that torch application should be performed by a CERTA (Certified Roofing Torch Applicator) . G GAF Useful manufacturer sources GAF — RUBEROID APP Torch-Applied Roofing Systems installation manual gaf.com — detailed application requirements, seam adhesion, torch technique, and safety. GAF — Torch-Down Roofing: Installation and Maintenance gaf.com — discusses maintenance and repairs to torch-applied modified-bitumen roofs. GAF — MATRIX 201 SBS Flashing Cement gaf.com — example of a compatible modified-bitumen repair/flashing material. PVC sheet membrane — best proven general-purpose option PVC membranes are widely used in tunnel waterproofing because they provide: High waterproofing reliability when seams are properly welded. Good flexibility and ability to accommodate some deformation. Heat-welded seams that can be inspected/tested. Compatibility with compartmentalized waterstops, allowing leaks to be isolated to manageable sections. A well-established installation methodology. For example, the U.S. Federal Transit Administration describes a tunnel system using a PVC synthetic geomembrane , with heat-welded seams and tested double-welded joints. F Federal Transit Administration FTA — Waterproofing and Its Effect on Operation and Maintenance of Underground Facilities transit.dot.gov 2. EVA membrane — excellent alternative, particularly where flexibility is important EVA (ethylene-vinyl acetate) membranes are also commonly specified for tunnels. They can provide high elongation and flexibility, which is valuable where the primary lining or surrounding ground may experience movement. Some tunnel specifications explicitly permit EVA or PVC membranes with a nonwoven geotextile layer . S Scribd The important point is that I wouldn't automatically say EVA is better than PVC. Both can be excellent; the project-specific specification and installation system matter more than the polymer name alone. What about HDPE? HDPE is highly durable and chemically resistant, but it is relatively stiff compared with flexible PVC/EVA systems. Consequently, detailing around penetrations, irregular tunnel profiles, joints and areas of movement can be more demanding. For a conventional mined tunnel where constructability and welded, inspectable seams are priorities, I'd generally start by evaluating PVC and EVA before HDPE . Spray-applied membranes A spray-applied waterproofing membrane can be the better solution in particular situations—especially where geometry is complicated, access is difficult, or a fully bonded membrane is desirable. ITAtech specifically provides design guidance for spray-applied waterproofing membranes in excavated tunnels and shafts. I ITA-AITES However, spray-applied systems are more sensitive to substrate preparation, application conditions, thickness/coverage and workmanship . ITAtech notes that high water ingress can also make some spray-applied systems impractical. FHWA emphasizes that tunnel waterproofing should be designed as an integrated system based on ground and groundwater conditions, tunnel geometry, construction method and ultimate use. It identifies two fundamental approaches: drained/open and undrained/closed systems. answerText: Yes. Some mineral-granule shedding from a brand-new SBS modified-bitumen membrane roll is normal , but excessive shedding can indicate a manufacturing or storage/handling problem. Why granules come off new SBS membrane Not every granule is intended to be permanently bonded. During manufacture, mineral granules are broadcast into the hot SBS-modified asphalt surface. Manufacturers commonly apply more granule than the surface can retain , so that the surface has complete coverage. IKO explicitly notes that excess mineral is used to obtain complete coverage and that loose granules can naturally fall away. [1] Handling and rolling abrades the surface. A finished membrane is wound tightly into a roll and subsequently moved, stored, unrolled and cut. Granules that are only partially embedded can be dislodged by friction between the membrane surface and adjacent layers of the roll, packaging, rollers, forklifts, etc. The roofing industry recognizes granule loss from abrasion as a measurable property. ASTM D4977 specifically tests granule adhesion by abrasion on “as manufactured” material . [2] Granule embedment is a key manufacturing variable. The granules need to become sufficiently embedded in the hot asphalt coating. If the asphalt temperature/viscosity, granule application rate, pressing/embedding pressure, or contact time is not well controlled, adhesion can be weaker. A published patent experiment on SBS cap sheets found that additional granule pressing substantially reduced measured granule loss, demonstrating the importance of the embedment/pressing operation. [3] Granule geometry and size matter. Granules that sit relatively high on the asphalt surface have less mechanical embedment and are more vulnerable to abrasion. This is consistent with observations from roofing-material evaluations that rounded/irregular granules can be more susceptible to loosening during handling and abrasion. [4] The membrane is designed with a surface treatment that differs by side. SBS membranes generally need a surface treatment that prevents the roll from sticking to itself. The RCABC Roofing Practices Manual explains that membranes are surface-treated with parting agents and that exposed surfaces can instead be protected with mineral granules. [5] This is why it is important to distinguish normal loose surface granules from actual failure of the granule-to-asphalt bond. When is it a concern? A light dusting or small amount of loose granule when first handling/unrolling a new roll is not necessarily a defect . In fact, manufacturers' installation instructions routinely tell installers to remove loose granules from lap areas before forming seams. Johns Manville, for example, specifically instructs installers to remove loose granules and then heat/embed the remaining granules at laps. [6] However, I would investigate it if you are seeing: substantial granule piles beneath/around the roll; large bare asphalt spots after ordinary handling; granules coming off with very light rubbing or brushing; a noticeable difference between rolls from the same production lot; exposed asphalt over significant portions of the weathering surface; or granule-loss testing that exceeds the applicable product specification. ASTM D4977/D4977M is particularly relevant because it is intended to evaluate the quality of adhesion of granular surfacing to the coating asphalt and expressly applies to material “as manufactured.” [7] For perspective, published roofing-industry testing has cited 2 g maximum granule loss for SBS/APP products under the applicable ASTM product standards, although the exact requirement depends on the membrane type and applicable standard. [8] A useful way to diagnose your particular rolls If you're investigating a production issue, I would separate the problem into three possibilities: Observation More likely explanation Small amount of loose granule immediately after unrolling Normal excess surface granule Mostly fines/dust, with granules otherwise firmly embedded Normal manufacturing/handling shedding Many intact granules readily coming off with rubbing Poor embedment/adhesion Problem concentrated in one production section or roll Manufacturing-process variation Problem increases dramatically with warm rolls Asphalt surface too soft / insufficiently set Granules transferred to the back of the next layer Excess surface granule and/or inadequate surface set Bare asphalt patches or visibly sparse coverage Potential manufacturing defect The most useful objective check is an ASTM D4977 granule-loss test on samples taken from the suspect new rolls , rather than judging the problem solely by how much granule you see on the floor. ASTM describes D4977 as an abrasion test specifically for this purpose. [9] Relevant sources ASTM D4977/D4977M — Standard Test Method for Granule Adhesion to Mineral-Surfaced Roofing by Abrasion — the key standard for quantifying granule adhesion on as-manufactured material. IKO Ultra Gold 20 Capsheet technical data sheet — explicitly discusses normal mineral shedding from newly manufactured mineral-coated membrane. RCABC Roofing Practices Manual — SBS Introduction — explains SBS membrane construction, surface treatments and mineral-granule surfacing. Johns Manville SBS Roofing Systems Application Guide — useful manufacturer guidance concerning loose granules and granule embedment. Research on durability of adhesion between bituminous coatings and mineral granules — scientific study of mineral-granule adhesion on SBS/APP bituminous membranes. Bottom line: a small amount of loose mineral on a new SBS roll is expected because the manufacturing process intentionally uses excess granule coverage. Heavy or easily induced granule loss, however, points toward inadequate granule embedment/adhesion, process-temperature or pressure issues, unsuitable granule characteristics, or abnormal handling/storage. ASTM D4977 provides the appropriate way to determine whether the observed loss is actually excessive. [10]

Bubbles or blisters appearing after torch application of an SBS (styrene-butadiene-styrene) modified-bitumen membrane are usually caused by trapped air/moisture or inadequate bonding, with the torch heat making the problem visible or causing it to grow. Why bubbles form Trapped moisture is the most common cause If the roof deck, insulation, primer, substrate, or underlying membrane contains moisture, torch heating raises its temperature rapidly. The moisture turns into water vapor and expands. Because the SBS membrane is relatively impermeable, the vapor can become trapped and push the membrane upward, creating a bubble/blister. Research by the National Research Council of Canada (NRC) found that gases inside SBS membrane blisters consisted mainly of air and water vapor , and concluded that water vapor can promote blister growth through repeated expansion and contraction as roof temperatures change. N NRC Publications +1 Voids or areas of incomplete adhesion If the membrane is not continuously bonded to the substrate, small pockets of air can remain underneath. When the torch heats the membrane and substrate, that trapped air expands and can form a bubble. NRC specifically identifies voids created during installation, uneven substrates, and inadequate bonding as contributors to blistering. N NRC Publications +1 Torching over a damp substrate Manufacturer instructions are quite explicit about this. Johns Manville's SBS application guide states that roofing materials should not be applied to wet or damp surfaces , because moisture trapped in the roofing system can cause damage. It also identifies moisture entrapment as a common cause of blistering. J Johns Manville A torch-grade SBS product data sheet likewise warns that residual moisture in the substrate and roofing materials can become trapped and cause blistering . M MBTechnology Too much or too concentrated heat Torch-applied SBS works by heating the underside bitumen until it becomes sufficiently fluid to bond to the substrate. If the flame is held too long in one location, the membrane can be overheated locally. This can rapidly generate vapor from residual moisture and create localized pockets before the membrane is properly set. The RCABC guidance says the membrane should be fully and evenly bonded and that sufficient heat should melt the bottom bitumen across the full width of the roll. R RCABC Roofing Practices Manual Moisture introduced during phased construction Leaving an underlying roofing layer exposed to weather before installing the next layer can allow moisture to enter the assembly. Johns Manville specifically warns that phased construction can result in moisture-entrapment blisters . J Johns Manville An important distinction A small, uniform bead/wave of melted asphalt ahead of the roll is actually an indication that adequate heat is being applied during torching. That is different from a raised bubble appearing behind the roll. RCABC's SBS standard describes the melted bitumen wave/bead in front of the roll as an indication of sufficient heat, while requiring the membrane to be fully and evenly bonded to its substrate. R RCABC Roofing Practices Manual What to check on the roof If bubbles are appearing immediately during or shortly after torching, I would investigate these items first: Substrate moisture — deck, insulation, base sheet, or existing membrane. Whether the surface was actually dry before torching. Primer condition and compatibility , where primer is required. Whether the membrane is fully bonding rather than bridging over voids. Torch technique — flame movement, distance, and heating pattern. Whether the underlying assembly was exposed to rain/dew overnight. Whether bubbles occur randomly or follow specific locations such as insulation joints, deck joints, laps, or low spots. If the bubbles are localized and appear almost immediately when the torch passes , trapped moisture/air or localized overheating is particularly worth investigating. If they develop or enlarge hours/days later , moisture trapped in the assembly and subsequent thermal expansion is a strong possibility. The right system depends heavily on whether you have a TBM/segmental tunnel, mined tunnel with a sprayed-concrete primary lining, or cut-and-cover station/tunnel , plus groundwater pressure and the required watertightness. My default recommendation For a conventional mined metro tunnel with a sprayed-concrete primary lining and cast-in-place secondary lining , a strong baseline specification is: Geotextile protection/drainage layer + flexible PVC or TPO sheet waterproofing membrane + welded joints + waterstops at construction joints. PVC sheet membranes are a particularly well-established tunnel solution. U.S. Federal Transit Administration guidance describes a system using a synthetic PVC sheet membrane , mechanically fixed to the tunnel, with overlapping sheets heat-welded at seams and PVC waterstops welded to the membrane at liner joints. It also identifies groundwater pressure, drainage strategy, maintenance and settlement risk as important factors in selecting the system. I ITA-AITES +1 For an urban metro , the drainage question is especially important: ITAtech notes that non-drained waterproofing systems are commonly used for urban metro running tunnels because permanently draining groundwater can potentially contribute to surface settlement and can create long-term maintenance issues. prompt: What is the best self-adhesive waterproofing membrane for underground structures? Please provide relevant web links or sources for your answer.

answerText: For commercial low-slope roofing , neither method is universally “better.” The better choice depends on the roof assembly, substrate, climate, installation conditions, fire restrictions, and the membrane manufacturer’s approved system. Quick comparison Factor Self-adhered membrane Torch-applied membrane Fire safety ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Excellent — no open flame ⭐⭐ Higher risk because of open flame Installation Generally simpler/cleaner Requires skilled torch application Speed Often fast, especially on smaller/detail-heavy jobs Can be very fast on large open areas Seam quality Excellent when properly rolled/prepared Excellent when properly torched Cold-weather installation More sensitive to temperature and substrate conditions Generally more tolerant, depending on product Odor/fumes Very low Low, but open-flame operation Labor skill Easier to train/install correctly Requires experienced installers Fire-watch/insurance issues Much less problematic Potentially significant Complex details Often advantageous Can provide excellent detailing with experienced crews Large, straightforward roofs Good Often highly productive My recommendation For most commercial projects today, I would favor self-adhered modified-bitumen membrane when the manufacturer-approved assembly can meet the project's performance requirements. The biggest reason is installation safety . Torch application uses an open propane flame, and the NRCA specifically warns about fire risk. NRCA recommends avoiding direct torching where potential fire hazards cannot be adequately mitigated and recommends CERTA-trained applicators for torch work. [1] Self-adhered systems eliminate that open-flame hazard. GAF Commercial also notes that self-adhered SBS membranes are popular because they produce virtually no odor and are typically faster to install. [2] When I'd choose torch-applied Torch-applied can still be an excellent commercial roofing system , particularly when: The roof is a large, uncomplicated area. The substrate is appropriate for torching. You have a highly experienced/certified crew. The project specifications favor a torch-applied assembly. Installation conditions make self-adhering performance less reliable. The manufacturer provides a strong warranty for the specific assembly. The important distinction is that torch-applied isn't inherently a lower-quality roof . NRCA says torch-applied polymer-modified bitumen products have been successfully used for decades; the concern is controlling the fire risk through proper design, detailing, and installation. [3] A particularly important issue: combustible substrates If you're roofing over wood decking, wood blocking, or other combustible materials , I'd lean strongly toward a non-torch application unless the complete assembly has been specifically designed for safe torch use. NRCA's guidance has become more conservative: it says the fire risk of torch-applied polymer-modified bitumen over combustible roof decks can outweigh the advantages of torch application, and it no longer recommends specifying direct torching over combustible roof decks. [4] One caveat with self-adhered Don't assume “peel-and-stick” automatically means easier or better . Self-adhered membranes depend heavily on proper substrate preparation, temperature, pressure/rolling, primers where specified, and seam detailing. A poorly installed self-adhered roof can be worse than a properly installed torch system. The NRCA defines self-adhering membrane as a membrane capable of adhering to the substrate and itself at overlaps without additional adhesive. [5] Bottom line If I were specifying a new commercial roof and had an otherwise equivalent choice: Self-adhered → my default choice for safety, simplicity, and reduced installation risk. Torch-applied → potentially preferable for certain large commercial assemblies where productivity, system design, and an experienced CERTA-qualified crew justify the open-flame method. And I would choose based on the complete tested/warranted roof assembly , not simply the membrane attachment method. Useful industry sources NRCA — Torch Safety Guidelines — discusses fire risks and recommended practices for torch-applied systems. NRCA — CERTA Program — information on training and fire-safe torch application. NRCA — Specifying the CERTA Program — guidance on when torching should be avoided and alternative application methods. GAF Commercial — Asphaltic Membrane Resources — comparison/background on SBS application methods, including self-adhered and torch-applied. NRCA — Modified Bitumen Systems Installer Certification — useful if you're evaluating contractor qualifications. If you tell me the building type, roof deck (metal, concrete, wood, etc.), approximate square footage, and whether this is new construction or reroofing , I can give you a more specific self-adhered vs. torch recommendation, including expected pros/cons and lifecycle considerations .

answerText: If you're comparing modified bitumen (mod-bit) with TPO for a flat or low-slope roof, the short answer is: Modified bitumen is usually cheaper upfront, but TPO is often more cost-effective over the full life of the roof—especially in a hot, sunny climate such as Phoenix. Cost comparison Factor Modified Bitumen TPO Typical installed cost* ~$4–$8/sq. ft. ~$5–$10/sq. ft. Typical service life ~15–25 years ~20–30 years Upfront cost Lower Higher Heat/UV performance Good, especially with reflective cap Excellent with white membrane Foot-traffic/puncture resistance Very good Good Repairs Generally straightforward Straightforward, but requires proper heat-welding Cooling-energy benefit Moderate Better Best value Lower initial budget / heavy traffic Long-term ownership / hot climates *Actual pricing varies substantially with roof size, insulation, tear-off, substrate condition, attachment method, membrane thickness and local labor. Current published 2026 estimates show overlapping ranges, so contractor bids are more meaningful than a generic national number. [1] Why TPO may win over time A white TPO membrane is highly reflective, which is particularly valuable in a hot climate. The U.S. Department of Energy notes that cool-roof products can provide meaningful lifetime energy savings, and TPO is commonly available in reflective white formulations. [2] TPO also tends to have a longer expected service life . Several 2026 comparisons put TPO around 20–30 years versus roughly 15–25 years for modified bitumen. [3] That doesn't automatically make TPO cheaper. For example, if your mod-bit bid is $4.50/sq. ft. and your TPO bid is $6.50/sq. ft., the mod-bit roof could still be the better choice if you're planning to sell the building or don't expect to keep it for 20+ years. When I'd choose modified bitumen Mod-bit makes more financial sense when: Your primary objective is the lowest initial installation cost . The roof receives substantial foot traffic or mechanical activity . You're replacing an existing mod-bit roof and the substrate/details are already configured for it. You value relatively easy localized repairs. The building's expected ownership period is relatively short. Its multi-ply asphalt construction gives it good resistance to punctures and traffic, which can be valuable around rooftop HVAC equipment. [4] When I'd choose TPO TPO makes more financial sense when: You're planning to own the property for 15–25+ years . The roof is exposed to intense sun and heat. answerText: Cold weather is a common cause of SBS membrane damage because the asphalt/polymer sheet becomes stiffer and less forgiving. SBS itself has good low-temperature flexibility, but installation handling and adhesion are still temperature-sensitive . [1] How to reduce tearing and cracking Keep the membrane warm until immediately before installation. Don't leave rolls sitting on a cold roof overnight. For example, SOPREMA recommends keeping membrane rolls around 70°F (21°C) in cold weather, while GAF specifies at least 45°F (7°C) for its RUBEROID SBS heat-weld systems. Your membrane manufacturer's PDS/manual takes precedence. [2] Condition and relax the rolls before laying them. In cooler weather, unroll the membrane and allow it to relax before final installation. GAF specifically recommends pre-unrolling/relaxing rolls to reduce wrinkles and says rolls can be cut into shorter lengths to make handling easier. [3] Avoid aggressively forcing a cold roll flat or sharply bending it around corners. Don't drag, sharply fold, or kink a cold sheet. Use adequate manpower or lifting/handling equipment so the membrane isn't stretched or folded while cold. Pay particular attention to corners, penetrations, end laps, and transitions—areas where concentrated bending can initiate a tear. Respect the minimum installation temperature. A useful general benchmark is 40°F (4°C) and rising , but the actual limit depends on the membrane and application method. Elevate, for example, specifies 40°F and rising for SBS/APP/BUR installation and recommends storing rolls at 50–100°F. SOPREMA recommends at least 40°F and rising for certain systems. [4] If conditions are below the manufacturer's limit, postponing installation is generally preferable to trying to compensate by mechanically forcing or excessively heating the membrane. Keep the substrate completely dry and frost-free. Ice, frost, dew and water can compromise adhesion and create conditions where the membrane gets damaged during installation. GAF specifically requires a dry substrate with no ice, dew, or water for cold-weather work. [5] Make sure adhesives and asphalt are at their specified application temperature. Cold adhesive can become too viscous to achieve proper coverage, while cold asphalt loses heat rapidly. GAF recommends maintaining the specified asphalt temperature rather than simply overheating it to compensate for cold ambient conditions. [6] For self-adhered SBS, pay particular attention to membrane temperature and rolling. Mule-Hide recommends membranes at 60–80°F (16–27°C) during installation and prompt rolling with a minimum 75-lb roller. [7] Minimize foot traffic and handling immediately after installation. Cold-weather systems can require additional time to develop adhesion. Avoid dragging tools/materials across the membrane and avoid unnecessary traffic until the assembly has adequately set. If you're specifically seeing tears If the sheet is tearing while you're unrolling or positioning it , the first things I'd investigate are: membrane temperature at the time of installation; whether the roll was stored/conditioned properly; whether it was sharply bent or kinked; whether the particular membrane has a manufacturer's cold-weather restriction; wind causing the sheet to fold or snap during handling; and whether you're trying to install below the manufacturer's minimum temperature. If the tear occurs during torching , that's a different problem: excessive torching/overheating or improper torch technique may be involved. GAF explicitly warns not to overheat SBS heat-weld rolls to compensate for cold ambient temperatures . [8] Useful manufacturer references GAF RUBEROID SBS Heat-Welded Roofing Systems Manual — Cold-Weather Application Precautions — particularly useful for roll conditioning, minimum temperatures, substrate conditions, and heat-weld application. SOPREMA SBS Membrane Roofing Technical Manual — detailed cold-weather requirements, including membrane/adhesive temperatures and substrate preparation. Elevate Cold Weather Application Guidelines — practical guidance for SBS/APP/BUR installation and material storage. Mule-Hide Self-Adhering Modified Bitumen Cold-Weather Guide — especially relevant if your SBS membrane is self-adhered. RCABC SBS Roofing Systems Standard — useful independent industry guidance emphasizing compliance with the membrane manufacturer's cold-weather storage/conditioning requirements. Bottom line: Don't try to make a cold SBS roll behave like a warm roll. Warm/condition the material, keep it dry, let it relax, handle it gently, stay within the manufacturer's temperature limits, and ensure the adhesive/weld conditions are correct. Those measures address most cold-weather tearing mechanisms.

answerText: If you’re writing a roofing specification for an SBS-modified bitumen membrane , I would generally specify 4 mm for the exposed cap membrane , rather than simply saying “3–4 mm.” My recommendation Specify 4.0 mm SBS membrane for the cap sheet unless the project’s selected roofing system/manufacturer specifically calls for 3 mm. Why: 4 mm is a common cap-sheet thickness. Sika, for example, lists a 4 mm SBS cap sheet alongside 3 mm SBS base plies. [1] 3 mm is commonly used as a base/interply. Sika's 3 mm E54 products are specifically identified as SBS-modified base plies . [2] RCABC's SBS roofing standards distinguish base and cap membranes and show cap-sheet minimum thicknesses around 3.3–4.0 mm depending on reinforcement and application method . [3] A 4 mm cap membrane generally gives you more material and mechanical robustness than a 3 mm membrane, although thickness alone isn't enough to establish performance —reinforcement, tensile/tear strength, puncture resistance, surfacing, application method, and the tested roof assembly matter too. GAF publishes dedicated SBS modified-bitumen master specifications, which is a good starting point for making the specification system-based rather than thickness-only . [4] What I'd put in the spec For a conventional 2-ply SBS roof, something along these lines is more defensible: SBS-modified bitumen roofing membrane, consisting of a manufacturer-approved base ply and 4.0 mm minimum SBS-modified bitumen cap sheet, reinforced with polyester, with membrane system complying with applicable ASTM requirements and the manufacturer's tested assembly. If you're specifying a single-ply SBS membrane , I'd be more cautious about automatically choosing 4 mm. There are systems where 3 mm is appropriate, and the governing code/roofing manufacturer/FM/UL assembly may dictate the thickness. Useful manufacturer/source links Sika — Modified Bitumen Roofing Sheets — shows actual 3 mm SBS base-ply and 4 mm SBS cap-sheet products. Sika — 3 mm SBS Base Ply — useful example of where 3 mm is used. GAF — SBS Modified Bitumen Master Specifications — manufacturer specification resources. RCABC — Standard for SBS-Modified Bitumen Membrane Systems — detailed thickness and membrane-system requirements. Bottom line: If you're choosing between 3 mm and 4 mm for the exposed SBS cap sheet, I'd specify 4 mm. If you tell me whether this is a 2-ply roof, single-ply roof, or waterproofing/grade-level application , I can recommend the exact thickness, reinforcement, ASTM standard, and spec language I would use.

answerText: When sourcing SBS modified-bitumen membrane from a Chinese factory , I would treat it as a technical procurement project rather than simply comparing price per roll. The biggest risks are incorrect reinforcement, insufficient SBS/polymer content, excessive filler, inconsistent coating weight, poor dimensional stability, and certificates that don't actually correspond to the product being supplied . Here is the due-diligence approach I'd use. 1. Start with a very precise product specification Before asking factories for prices, issue your own specification covering: Membrane type: SBS torch-applied, self-adhered, cold-applied, etc. Application: roofing, below-grade waterproofing, foundation, plaza deck, etc. Thickness: e.g. 3 mm, 4 mm, 5 mm. Width and roll length Reinforcement: polyester, fiberglass, or polyester + fiberglass. Surface: mineral/granule, sand, film, aluminum, etc. SBS polymer content or, preferably, the performance requirements that the formulation must achieve. Tensile strength and elongation Tear strength Low-temperature flexibility Heat resistance/flow Dimensional stability Water absorption Coating weight/mass per unit area Thickness tolerances Roll/core dimensions Packaging and pallet requirements. For North American roofing/waterproofing, ASTM D6162, D6163 and D6164 are particularly useful starting points. ASTM D6164, for example, covers SBS sheets using polyester reinforcement and specifies properties including thickness, mass per unit area, tensile performance, elongation, tear strength, low-temperature flexibility, dimensional stability, compound stability and granule embedment. A ASTM Store ASTM D6164/D6164M — SBS sheets with polyester reinforcement store.astm.org ASTM D6162/D6162M — polyester + glass reinforcement store.astm.org ASTM D6163/D6163M — glass-fiber reinforcement store.astm.org 2. Don't accept "SBS" as proof of formulation quality This is one of the most important checks. Ask the factory to provide a complete formulation/material declaration , including: Asphalt source and grade SBS polymer manufacturer and grade SBS dosage/content Mineral filler type and percentage Reinforcement specification Surface coating/granule specification Any APP, rubber, plastomer or other polymer modification Process oil/additives, where applicable. I would be cautious if the factory refuses to disclose even the polymer manufacturer and approximate SBS percentage . Also compare the claimed formulation against the physical test results. A factory can claim a high SBS content while producing a membrane whose low-temperature flexibility, heat resistance or tensile performance doesn't support the claim. 3. Verify the reinforcement For a membrane, the reinforcement is just as important as the asphalt compound. Ask for: Reinforcement manufacturer Polyester/fiberglass type Basis weight Tensile strength Orientation Whether it is centrally positioned Coating penetration through the reinforcement Reinforcement weight per square meter. For example, ASTM D6162 specifically covers a combination of polyester fabric and glass-fiber reinforcement, whereas D6164 is primarily polyester reinforced. A ASTM Store +1 Request an actual cross-section sample , rather than relying on photographs. A good inspection company can cut a roll cross-section and verify whether the reinforcement is centered and uniformly saturated. 4. Require independent laboratory testing Don't rely solely on the manufacturer's COA. This is probably the single most valuable safeguard when buying from an unfamiliar factory. Have samples from the actual production lot tested by an independent laboratory for the applicable ASTM specification. ASTM D5147 provides test methods for modified-bitumen sheets, including sampling, tensile/elongation, tear, moisture, water absorption, dimensional stability, low-temperature flexibility, heat conditioning, weathering, coating thickness, granule embedment and compound stability. A ASTM Store ASTM D5147/D5147M — Sampling and testing modified-bitumen sheet store.astm.org I'd do this at three stages: Before purchase: Test factory samples. During first production: Third-party inspector takes samples directly from production. For subsequent shipments: Randomly test selected lots rather than trusting every COA. 5. Pay particular attention to low-temperature flexibility For SBS membrane, this is a major performance indicator. Ask for the actual test temperature and result—not simply: "Low temperature flexibility: Pass." For example, require: Low-temperature flexibility: ≤ X °C, tested according to specified ASTM method. Then have the laboratory verify it. This is especially useful for detecting a membrane that has been made cheaper through formulation changes or excessive filler. ASTM's SBS specifications specifically include low-temperature flexibility among the required material properties. A ASTM Store +1 6. Check coating weight, not just nominal thickness A factory can produce a nominal "4 mm" membrane that doesn't contain the same amount of useful bituminous compound as another manufacturer's 4 mm product. Specify both: Thickness Net mass per unit area and establish tolerances. ASTM D6162/D6164 explicitly incorporate dimensional and mass requirements, so these are much better purchasing controls than simply specifying "4 mm SBS membrane." A ASTM Store +1 I'd also weigh complete rolls and calculate: net membrane weight ÷ actual membrane area = kg/m² rather than accepting the factory's stated number. 7. Investigate the factory—not just the trading company Determine whether you're dealing with: Actual manufacturer Trading company Manufacturer + export company Factory producing under another company's certification. Ask for: Chinese legal company name Unified Social Credit Code Factory address Business license Export history Production-line photographs/video Number and type of production lines Annual capacity Main export markets Major customers, if they can disclose them Raw-material suppliers QC laboratory equipment Recent production records. Then verify that the company named on the certificate, test report, invoice and factory address are consistent . A surprisingly common procurement mistake is qualifying a trading company while believing you've qualified the factory. 8. Audit the production line If the order is significant, I'd strongly recommend a physical factory audit. Look at: Raw materials Are SBS pellets actually present? Are raw materials stored properly? Are batches identified? Is asphalt coming from consistent sources? Mixing Automated weighing? Temperature control? Mixing time? Batch records? Coating Automated thickness control? Continuous monitoring? Temperature control? Reinforcement alignment? Cooling Is the sheet properly cooled before winding? Winding Consistent roll tension? Telescoping? Wrinkling? Edge alignment? Laboratory Tensile tester Thickness gauge Low-temperature flexibility equipment Heat-aging equipment Dimensional-stability testing Mass/basis-weight measurement. A factory that can't demonstrate meaningful in-house QC deserves considerably more scrutiny. 9. Verify every certificate Be particularly careful with: ASTM compliance certificates CE certificates ISO 9001 UL listings FM approvals Factory test reports SGS/Bureau Veritas/Intertek reports. ISO 9001 does not prove that the membrane meets your performance specification. Likewise, an ASTM test report isn't necessarily evidence that your product complies unless you establish that the tested product, formulation, reinforcement, factory and manufacturing process correspond to the product you're buying. Ask: "Please provide the complete laboratory report for the exact product and construction we are purchasing, including product designation, thickness, reinforcement, factory address, sample identification and test date." Then independently verify the report with the laboratory. 10. Check fire and system approvals separately This is an easy one to overlook. ASTM D6162/D6164 are material specifications . They do not, by themselves, establish the performance of the entire roof assembly—for example fire resistance, uplift resistance, impact resistance or compatibility with a particular roof system. ASTM explicitly notes these limitations. A ASTM Store +1 So if you're selling the membrane into a particular roofing market, determine whether you need things such as: UL classification/listing FM approval ASTM E108/UL 790 fire performance Wind-uplift testing System-specific approvals Local building-code compliance. Don't let a factory say "ASTM certified" and assume that means the complete roofing system is approved. 11. Inspect actual production rolls For the first shipment, I would use a third-party inspection company in China. Have them randomly select rolls and check: Roll count Roll dimensions Weight Thickness at multiple locations Width Surface appearance Edge straightness Wrinkles Telescoping Core condition Labeling Batch numbers Packaging Water damage Manufacturing date. Then retain sealed samples from the shipment . That's important because if a dispute occurs six months later, you want evidence of what was actually shipped. 12. Put the specification into the purchase contract Don't make the supplier's quotation the technical specification. Your PO/contract should identify: Product → exact construction → applicable standard → required test values → tolerances → sampling procedure → third-party inspection → rejection criteria. I'd also include a clause stating that changes to asphalt grade, SBS supplier, SBS dosage, reinforcement, filler, production site or formulation require written approval . This prevents the classic situation where the factory supplies a good sample and then quietly substitutes cheaper raw materials after receiving the order. 13. Watch for these red flags I'd consider these significant warning signs: 🚩 Extremely low price compared with established Chinese manufacturers. 🚩 Factory won't identify the SBS polymer supplier. 🚩 "SBS membrane" but no meaningful formulation information. 🚩 Test reports supplied only as screenshots. 🚩 Certificates issued to a different company/address. 🚩 Test report is several years old. 🚩 Report doesn't state reinforcement or thickness. 🚩 Factory refuses third-party inspection. 🚩 Factory refuses independent testing. 🚩 COA values are suspiciously identical for every production batch. 🚩 Factory offers to "make the certificate match the customer's specification." 🚩 Sample is excellent but production inspection reveals different construction. 🚩 Large discrepancies between nominal thickness and kg/m². A practical qualification sequence For a serious commercial purchase, I'd use this sequence: Factory shortlist → technical questionnaire → documentation verification → sample → independent laboratory test → factory audit → pilot order → pre-shipment inspection → independent shipment testing → full production approval. And I would not make the final supplier decision on price until the membrane has passed independent testing . Useful standards/resources The most useful starting references I found are: ASTM D6162/D6162M-21 store.astm.org — SBS membrane with polyester + glass reinforcement. ASTM D6163/D6163M-21 store.astm.org — SBS membrane with glass-fiber reinforcement. ASTM D6164/D6164M-21 store.astm.org — SBS membrane with polyester reinforcement. ASTM D5147/D5147M-18(2024) store.astm.org — sampling and laboratory testing of modified-bitumen sheet materials. ASTM roofing standards directory store.astm.org — useful for identifying related ASTM standards. One important update: ASTM's current standards directory also lists D6164/D6164M-26 , so if you're writing a new procurement specification in 2026, I'd verify the latest edition rather than automatically copying an older 2021 reference. A ASTM Store If you're sourcing this for the U.S. market , I can also give you a factory-vetting questionnaire + SBS membrane technical specification + pre-shipment inspection checklist , including the exact tests and acceptance limits I'd put into an RFQ/PO. answerText: SBS (styrene-butadiene-styrene) modified-bitumen membrane rolls should generally be stored upright, dry, protected from weather and sunlight, and handled carefully . Manufacturer instructions take precedence for the specific product. Recommended storage practices Keep rolls upright/on end. Do not store SBS membrane rolls lying flat on their sides. Upright storage helps prevent deformation and damage to the roll. GAF, SOPREMA, Sika, and Johns Manville all specify upright storage for their SBS products. G GAF +3 Store them on a firm, level, raised surface. Keep the rolls off the ground and supported so they cannot tip or become distorted. Some manufacturers specifically call for raised platforms or pallets. K Kemper System +1 Keep them dry and protected from weather. Ideally, use a clean, dry, weatherproof storage area. If outdoor storage is unavoidable, protect the rolls from rain, snow and moisture with an appropriate weather-resistant/opaque cover. Don't allow water to become trapped under an impermeable cover. S SOPREMA US +1 Protect from direct sunlight and excessive heat. Prolonged UV exposure and high temperatures can damage or deform some products. Sika, for example, specifically recommends avoiding direct sunlight during storage. S Sika UK +1 Avoid extreme cold and follow the manufacturer's temperature requirements. SBS membranes can become less flexible in cold conditions. Some manufacturers recommend conditioning rolls above about 50°F (10°C) before installation, particularly during cold weather. S SOPREMA US +2 Don't drop, drag, or roughly handle the rolls. Lift rather than drag them across rough surfaces, and take particular care when unloading in cold weather. Mechanical impacts can damage the roll or its edges. S Sika UK +1 Keep the original packaging intact until needed. Keeping factory packaging in place provides additional protection against moisture and physical damage. For self-adhered products, pay particular attention to the manufacturer's instructions because the release film/packaging can be important to storage performance. S Scribd +1 Don't overload or stack rolls improperly. Some SBS manufacturers explicitly prohibit stacking rolls more than one high; requirements vary by product. Follow the particular product's technical data sheet rather than assuming rolls can be stacked. M MBTechnology +1 A good practical setup For a jobsite, a good arrangement is: Pallet/raised platform → rolls standing vertically on their ends → stable support against tipping → original wrapping intact → opaque/weather-resistant cover → dry, shaded, well-ventilated location. answerText: If you mean exposed SBS modified-bitumen roofing , with one membrane having a mineral-granule surface and the other having a fine sand surface , the mineral-granule-surfaced membrane generally lasts longer when left exposed . Why The key difference is UV protection: Mineral granules are specifically intended to provide a durable exposed surface and shield the SBS-modified asphalt from ultraviolet radiation. The Roofing Contractors Association of British Columbia notes that exposed SBS membranes use mineral granules as UV protection. R RCABC Roofing Practices Manual A technical study of SBS and APP membranes found that mineral granules form the principal barrier against UV degradation and that the durability of the granule layer contributes to the membrane's service life. S ScienceDirect Sand-surfaced SBS is commonly used where the surface will be covered by another roofing layer or where the membrane is being used as a base/underlayment. It isn't generally intended to provide the same level of long-term exposed UV protection. RCABC specifically distinguishes sanded surfaces used for hot-asphalt application from exposed surfaces protected with mineral granules. R RCABC Roofing Practices Manual Practical comparison Feature Mineral-granule SBS Sand-surfaced SBS Long-term UV protection Excellent Limited Intended for exposed roof surface Yes Generally no Resistance to weathering Better Lower when exposed Typical application Cap sheet / exposed roof Base sheet / concealed layer Expected life when properly installed and maintained Longer Shorter if exposed As a real-world reference, GAF currently offers SBS mineral-granule membranes with 15-year typical system guarantees and, for selected constructions, up to 20 years . G GAF +1 Johns Manville likewise describes its SBS mineral-surfaced cap sheet as being engineered for durability and optimal granule embedment . J Johns Manville Important caveat: The membrane's reinforcement, thickness, SBS formulation, installation quality, roof slope/drainage, climate, foot traffic, and maintenance can have as much or more effect on actual life than the surface finish. So I wouldn't say, for example, that a particular granule membrane will automatically last twice as long as a particular sand-surfaced membrane. Bottom line: If these are otherwise comparable SBS membranes and you're choosing a surface for a roof that will remain exposed to the weather, choose the mineral-granule surface . If the membrane will be covered by another layer, sand-surfaced SBS can be entirely appropriate .
